meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'The best government is that which governs least'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Jefferson. The exact wording is an 1837 magazine motto from the Democratic Review; Thoreau borrowed a variant in 1849; Jefferson misattribution dates to ~1853.

answer.label: Not Thomas Jefferson — an 1837 magazine motto
answer.authorName: The United States Magazine and Democratic Review (John L. O’Sullivan, ed.)
answer.authorDates: Motto first printed 1837 · popularized in variant form by Henry David Thoreau, 1849
answer.sourceLine: The Thomas Jefferson Foundation at Monticello lists this among Jefferson’s spurious quotations ↗ — it appears nowhere in his writings. The exact wording, “The best government is that which governs least,” was printed as a motto in the first issue of the United States Magazine and Democratic Review in 1837, and Henry David Thoreau borrowed the variant “That government is best which governs least” to open Civil Disobedience (1849), explicitly calling it a “motto” he was quoting.

source.excerptNote: As printed in the introductory statement of the Democratic Review (1837). Thoreau’s 1849 variant reads: “I heartily accept the motto, — ‘That government is best which governs least’…” — his own words marking it as a pre-existing motto, not his coinage.

author.name: John L. O’Sullivan & the Democratic Review
author.heading: The real origin of the wording
author.metaLine: United States Magazine and Democratic Review, est. 1837 · ed. John L. O’Sullivan (1813–1895)
author.bio: The exact line — “The best government is that which governs least” — first appears as an editorial motto in the debut 1837 issue of the United States Magazine and Democratic Review, the Jacksonian journal founded and edited by John L. O’Sullivan (later famous for coining “Manifest Destiny”). Henry David Thoreau adapted the slightly different phrasing to open Civil Disobedience in 1849, expressly calling it a “motto” he accepted rather than one he invented. Neither Jefferson nor John Locke, to whom it is also sometimes credited, is known to have written it.

Monticello lists the Jefferson attribution as spurious.

misattribution.heading: Who it’s wrongly pinned on
misattribution.intro: This is one of the most persistently misattributed lines in American politics — cited by public officials as Jefferson’s to this day.

items.why: Monticello’s research team places the line among Jefferson’s spurious quotations ↗: it appears in none of his writings. It was likely attached to him because the sentiment suited his Democratic-Republican heirs; the earliest known Jefferson attribution dates to about 1853.

Thoreau opened Civil Disobedience (1849) with the variant “That government is best which governs least,” but his own text calls it a “motto” he “heartily accept[s]” — he was quoting an existing phrase ↗, not originating it.
Sometimes floated as the originator, but the wording is not found in Locke’s writings either.

misattribution.truthLine: The exact wording is an 1837 editorial motto from the Democratic Review; Thoreau borrowed a variant in 1849; Jefferson never wrote it, as fact-checkers ↗ and Monticello confirm.

context.heading: Why the mix-up sticks
lead: The phrase reads like a distilled statement of small-government philosophy, so it naturally gravitates toward the Founder most associated with limited federal power. But Jefferson’s actual writings never contain it — the wording postdates him.

Its real home is Jacksonian journalism: the masthead sentiment of the Democratic Review in 1837, then popularized when Thoreau adapted it a dozen years later. The attribution to Jefferson is a later back-formation, first documented around 1853.
context.pull: Jefferson never wrote it — it’s an 1837 magazine motto that Thoreau later borrowed.
